title: Caring for yourself as a carer
word: Caring for yourself as a carer

cards: The phone lights up at the edge of the bed: Mom needs her pills sorted, the kids need lunches, a friend needs a call back, and work needs that thing by noon.
Somewhere at the very bottom of the list, below the dog's vet appointment, there's a line that never quite gets written: rest.
People who look after others, a parent, a nurse, someone caring for a sick partner, may know the shape of that list. Today asks a quieter question: who's on the list of people that care is for?

teach.b: First, a circle with you in it. A few days ago, the Stoic Hierocles drew his circles of concern: family, neighbors, humanity. At the very center, he put the self.
Not to crown it, but because it's where every ring starts. A caregiver who leaves the center empty has nothing for the rings to grow from.
Second, a teacher who sent his friends to rest, in a line this path met on day eight hundred sixty-nine.

teach.h: COME APART AND REST A WHILE.
teach.b: In the Gospel of Mark, the disciples come back from their work, crowded and busy, and Jesus says, in the King James words: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while."
Mark adds the reason: so many were coming and going that they had no time even to eat. Rest, given as an instruction, in the middle of the work. Third, kindness that starts at home.
In the Visuddhimagga, the Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa describes developing loving-kindness by beginning with oneself, then moving out to others.
His reasoning: once you see that you want to be happy, you can see that others want it too. Fourth, the modern version.

Kristin Neff's research on self-compassion describes treating yourself with the kindness you would give a friend, recognizing that struggle is part of being human, and noticing pain without being swept away.
In that account, self-compassion isn't selfishness, and it isn't giving up on others.

teach.h: ONE MORE PERSON IN THE CARE.
teach.b: It includes one more person in the care: the one doing the caring.

how: In loving-kindness practice as Buddhaghosa describes it, the wish for well-being begins with oneself before moving outward, and self-compassion programs teach caregivers to offer themselves the kindness they give others.

o: putting yourself ahead of the people you look after
hiring help so you can stop caring for others

games.q: you've spent the day caring for a sick parent. there are ten free minutes before the next thing. what do you do?
o: catch up on chores so tomorrow is easier.
rest, with nothing to fix, and count it as part of the care.
feel guilty and scroll your phone.
games.why: in Mark's Gospel, rest comes as an instruction in the middle of the work. compassion includes the one who gives it.

practice: Drop the shoulders, unclench the jaw, let the breath go slow, and let the people you look after rest in the back of your mind, one by one.
Then turn the same care toward yourself, the hands that do the carrying, the tired back, the full head, with a hand on your chest if it helps: for this short time, nobody needs anything from you.

wordCard.voice: Caring for yourself as a carer. Compassion includes the one who gives it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: me too. When the wish goes out, may they be well, there's room for two more words. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
